**The all-in-one open-source enterprise AI platform.** *Built on a strong security and observability foundation: SSO and RBAC, sandboxed code execution, Dual-LLM and Lethal-Trifecta guardrails, OpenTelemetry traces, and Prometheus metrics — first-class, not bolted on.* [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-AGPL%203.0%20%2F%20Enterprise-blue.svg)](LICENSE.md) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/archestra-ai/archestra)](https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/releases) [![Contributors](https://img.shields.io/github/contributors/archestra-ai/archestra)](https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/graphs/contributors) [![Last commit](https://img.shields.io/github/last-commit/archestra-ai/archestra)](https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/commits/main) [![Commit activity](https://img.shields.io/github/commit-activity/m/archestra-ai/archestra)](https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/pulse) [Quickstart](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-quickstart)  ·  [Docs](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-overview)  ·  [Releases](https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/releases)  ·  [Slack](https://archestra.ai/join-slack)
--- ## What it does Point your users — or your agents, or Claude / Codex / Cursor — at one URL. Archestra handles the rest: - 💬 **Chat for non-technical users.** Internal AI assistant with [projects](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-projects), [MCP apps](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-apps), and [Slack](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-slack), [MS Teams](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-ms-teams), and [email](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-agent-triggers-email) front-ends. - 🛠️ **Developer LLM & MCP portal.** One token for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor — see the [proxy](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-llm-proxy). - 🚪 **LLM gateway** for [any provider](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-supported-llm-providers) (Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Bedrock, DeepSeek, …) with [cost limits](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-costs-and-limits), [virtual API keys](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-llm-proxy-authentication), and [dynamic model routing](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-model-router-client-credentials-example). - 🔌 **MCP gateway** with [OAuth + On-Behalf-Of](https://archestra.ai/docs/mcp-authentication) so tools run as the user, not a shared service account. - 🤝 **A2A gateway** for [agent-to-agent triggers](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-agent-triggers-webhook-a2a). - 📦 **Private MCP registry** so teams ship their own tools — see [registry docs](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-private-registry). - 🎼 **MCP orchestrator** with a [Kubernetes operator](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-orchestrator) and [self-serve promotion](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-environments). - 🤖 **Agent runtime** with [scheduled / email / webhook triggers](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-agents), [sub-agent delegation](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-agents), [reusable skills](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-agent-skills-sharing), sandboxed code execution, and a K8s-native filesystem. - 📚 **RAG knowledge base** plumbed via [connectors](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-knowledge-connectors) to your existing stack. - 🧩 **Mini app builder** — see [apps](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-apps). - 🛡️ **Deterministic guardrails** for [tool calls](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-ai-tool-guardrails), [Dual-LLM](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-built-in-subagents#dual-llm-agent) verification, and [Lethal Trifecta](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-ai-tool-guardrails#the-lethal-trifecta) protections. - 🪪 **Identity & access** with [SSO](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-sso) (OIDC, SAML, Okta, Entra), [RBAC with role mapping & team sync](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-access-control), and [secrets management](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-secrets-management). - 🌎 **Environments** with [per-env egress policies](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-environments) and [per-env cost limits](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-costs-and-limits). - 🔭 **Observability** out of the box: OpenTelemetry traces, Prometheus metrics, logs, [per-team cost tracking](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-costs-and-limits). > Already running dangerous single-tenant agents like Claude Cowork, > OpenClaw, or Hermes in your enterprise? **[Migration Kit →](migration-kit/README.md)** ## Quickstart ```bash docker pull archestra/platform:latest docker run \ -p 127.0.0.1:9000:9000 -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 \ -e ARCHESTRA_QUICKSTART=true \ -e ARCHESTRA_BETA=true \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ -v archestra-postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \ -v archestra-app-data:/app/data \ archestra/platform ``` Open . Full Docker / Helm / Kubernetes instructions live in the [quickstart docs](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-quickstart). ## Ready for production - ✅ $13.5M total funding - ✅ Three Fortune-50 deployments - ✅ 31 ms at p95 — [performance benchmarks →](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-performance-benchmarks) - ✅ [Terraform provider →](https://github.com/archestra-ai/terraform-provider-archestra) - ✅ [Helm chart →](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-deployment#helm-deployment-recommended-for-production) ## Deeper docs - 📖 [**Platform overview**](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-overview) — what's in the box, how the pieces fit together. - 📐 [**Deployment**](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-deployment) — Docker, Helm, Kubernetes, every env var, secrets management. - 💰 [**Pricing model**](https://archestra.ai/docs/platform-pricing-model) — Open Core, free for teams under 30 users, enterprise licensing. - 🛡️ [**Security & bug bounty**](https://archestra.ai/docs/security) - 🤝 [**Contributing**](https://archestra.ai/docs/contributing) — set up the dev env, run e2e tests, open a PR. Thank you for continuously making **Archestra** better — you're awesome 🫶 ---

[{"sha":"2feed0ce9363debe4df6b0d0829639bd5f383299","html_url":"https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/commit/2feed0ce9363debe4df6b0d0829639bd5f383299","commit":{"message":"fix(apps): bound app tool calls at the LLM ceiling and cancel abandoned calls (#6963) ## Summary An app's `archestra.llm.complete()` rejected with `MCP error -32001: Request timed out` whenever the attached model needed more than 60 seconds — which reasoning models routinely do, since the app path is the platform's only non-streaming LLM call and all thinking time accumulates into the single response (T-981). The timer was the MCP SDK's default request timeout in the app iframe's guest client: the SDK passed no request options to `callServerTool`, and nothing downstream was stricter, so the guest always lost the race while the backend kept generating (and the proxy kept billing) a result nobody would receive. Live measurement on a dev stack: the app showed the error at exactly 60s while the same completion returned HTTP 200 at 100s and was recorded in LLM logs ~40s after the app had already failed. The guest now bounds host tool calls at 10 minutes, matching the platform's own upstream LLM client ceiling (`ANTHROPIC_CLIENT_TIMEOUT_MS`) rather than gating stricter than it. Cancellation travels the whole chain: the guest's timeout or teardown aborts the host bridge's fetch via the `oncalltool` handler's `extra.signal`; the app proxy route closes the per-request transport when the client disconnects, which makes the protocol abort the in-flight handler's signal; that signal reaches `executeArchestraTool` (as the existing `context.abortSignal`) and `executeToolCallForOwner` (its existing `abortSignal` option); and an aborted LLM completion stops quietly instead of logging an error and claiming `llm_unavailable`. Two route-level details deserve reviewer attention. In JSON-response mode an aborted handler never produces a response, so `transport.handleRequest` never settles — the route races it against the client-disconnect path instead of awaiting it bare. And an aborted request leaves its transport closed mid-flight, so the per-(app,user) cached server is evicted rather than released for reuse; the cache's exclusive `acquire` guarantees the closed transport can only ever belong to the aborted request. ## Validation - `app-sdk-runtime.test.ts`: the guest-module stub now honors the MCP SDK's request-options timeout contract; new tests pin that a 3-minute completion resolves (red before this fix, failing with the exact reported error) and that a completion beyond the 10-minute ceiling still times out. - `app-llm.test.ts`: an aborted call cancels the model call and reports cancellation, not a provider failure. - Live on a dev stack with a reasoning model (glm-5.1): a 188-second completion resolves in the real iframe chain where it previously died at 60s; killing the viewer 25 seconds into a call produced the cancelled tool-call record within ~1 second. ## Follow-up The LLM proxy's non-streaming handlers do not tie their own upstream request to their client's disconnect, so a cancelled completion can still run to completion inside the proxy and record the interaction (observed landing two minutes after the abort). That gap predates this change, spans every provider adapter, and equally affects non-streamed chat cancellation — left for its own change. No docs change: the apps page never promised a timeout, and the fix restores its documented behavior (`llm.complete` resolves to the model's text). --- ","author":{"name":"Mark Novikov","email":"piercypixel@gmail.com","date":"2026-07-29T16:51:18Z"},"committer":{"name":"GitHub","email":"noreply@github.com","date":"2026-07-29T16:51:18Z"}},"author":{"login":"piercypixel","id":13911621,"profile_url":"https://github.com/piercypixel","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/13911621?v=4"},"committer":{"login":"web-flow","id":19864447,"profile_url":"https://github.com/web-flow","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/19864447?v=4"}},{"sha":"1dd549c91308beee38066bbc75e1baaf7af97ebc","html_url":"https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/commit/1dd549c91308beee38066bbc75e1baaf7af97ebc","commit":{"message":"fix(github-copilot): verify model invocability at sync, surface an actionable model-not-supported error (#6964) Fixes T-959: chat on the GitHub Copilot provider could fail with `400 {"message": "The requested model is not supported.", "type": "api_validation_error"}` for models Archestra itself offered in the model picker. ## Root cause Copilot's `/models` is not an invocability catalog. Verified against a live subscription: 13 of the 24 entries our static filter kept were rejected outright by `/chat/completions` with `model_not_supported` — retired aliases listed next to their still-working snapshots (`gpt-4` vs `gpt-4o`, `gpt-3.5-turbo` vs `gpt-3.5-turbo-0613`), client-internal agent models (`copilot-search-*`, `exec-agent-*`), and per-plan-unavailable models that still declare `"/chat/completions"` in `supported_endpoints`. No catalog field discriminates dead from alive entries (a dead alias can be field-identical to a working model, down to `version`), and on the verified plan every entry is `model_picker_enabled: false`, so no static filter can compute the usable set. GitHub's own clients avoid the problem only because their picker never exposes these entries. ## Fix **Verify invocability during model sync.** CAPI validates the model before the payload, so a deliberately invalid `{"model": …, "messages": []}` request is a zero-inference oracle: a dead model answers `model_not_supported`, a live one answers "messages must be non-empty". Nothing is generated and no model is ever invoked, so the probe cannot consume premium requests. The fetcher now probes every statically-kept candidate (8 concurrent) and drops only definite `model_not_supported` answers — 429/5xx/network failures keep the model, so an upstream outage degrades to the previous unverified catalog rather than an empty one. Runs everywhere the fetcher is used: connect-time key validation, lazy re-sync, explicit sync, and the proxy `/models` listing. **Actionable error for the residual window.** A conversation can stay pinned to a model that has since died (the proxy's error wrapping keeps `message`/`type` but drops the upstream `code`). The chat error mapper now classifies Copilot's model-not-supported 400 as `NotFound` — "The selected model is not available. Please choose a different model." — instead of the retry-suggesting invalid-request copy, which misleads on a deterministic rejection. ## Testing - New proxy route tests drive the real adapter and Copilot fetch wrapper (token exchange + editor-identity headers) against a faked wire, pinning that the catalogued model name goes upstream and the upstream 400 surfaces for both streaming and non-streaming. - New chat stream test pins that a github-copilot conversation's model FK is dereferenced to the provider model name before dispatch. - Fetcher tests cover the verification: a listed-but-rejected model is dropped, probes only target statically-kept candidates, inconclusive probes (429/network) keep the model. - Error-mapper tests cover the NotFound classification and that other Copilot 400s keep the generic invalid-request code. - Live validation on a dev stack with a real subscription: synced catalog went from 24 models (13 dead) to the invocable set; picking any listed model chats successfully; a conversation pinned to a dead model shows the actionable copy. --- ","author":{"name":"Mark Novikov","email":"piercypixel@gmail.com","date":"2026-07-29T16:45:51Z"},"committer":{"name":"GitHub","email":"noreply@github.com","date":"2026-07-29T16:45:51Z"}},"author":{"login":"piercypixel","id":13911621,"profile_url":"https://github.com/piercypixel","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/13911621?v=4"},"committer":{"login":"web-flow","id":19864447,"profile_url":"https://github.com/web-flow","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/19864447?v=4"}},{"sha":"1a1fd231e171822cd869f84c7e3346b59e76fbfb","html_url":"https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/commit/1a1fd231e171822cd869f84c7e3346b59e76fbfb","commit":{"message":"ci: revert run heavy test suites only in the merge queue (#6615) (#6801) Restores the heavy test suites (backend unit test shards + gate, frontend integration tests, and both Rust checks) to run on pull_request pushes again, reverting PR #6615 which had moved them to merge-queue-only behind a run-unit-tests label. This regressed dev experience: contributors could no longer confirm their tests passed on their own branch and instead had to iterate through the merge queue, where "new tests showing up" is unexpected. The original author-based bot-pr-guard is restored on each suite (bot PRs still skip), the `labeled` trigger and run-unit-tests escape hatch are removed, and later mac-mini runner routing plus the mac-mini-watchdog job are preserved untouched. Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Mc1gaHM4iHWsFeBYK7M9sg --- Co-authored-by: Claude Co-authored-by: Joey Orlando ","author":{"name":"Ildar Iskhakov","email":"ildar6v@gmail.com","date":"2026-07-29T15:22:41Z"},"committer":{"name":"GitHub","email":"noreply@github.com","date":"2026-07-29T15:22:41Z"}},"author":{"login":"iskhakov","id":2262529,"profile_url":"https://github.com/iskhakov","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/2262529?v=4"},"committer":{"login":"web-flow","id":19864447,"profile_url":"https://github.com/web-flow","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/19864447?v=4"}},{"sha":"2cb4a589217f3511054924e1e5e8e5de7b290b72","html_url":"https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/commit/2cb4a589217f3511054924e1e5e8e5de7b290b72","commit":{"message":"chore(mcp): stop declaring the roots capability no client implements (#6960) Follow-up nit from the #6953 chat-client review. All three MCP client constructions (chat loopback client, both upstream client paths in `mcp-client.ts`) declared `roots: { listChanged: true }` — but no `roots/list` handler exists anywhere in this codebase, so a server acting on the declaration always got method-not-found. Roots is also deprecated in 2026-07-28. Removing a client capability only reduces what servers attempt; nothing that worked can break. Verified: `tsc`, `biome ci`, `knip` clean; 157 tests across `mcp-client` and the chat-client suites pass. --- ","author":{"name":"Joey Orlando","email":"joey@archestra.ai","date":"2026-07-29T14:51:50Z"},"committer":{"name":"GitHub","email":"noreply@github.com","date":"2026-07-29T14:51:50Z"}},"author":{"login":"joeyorlando","id":9406895,"profile_url":"https://github.com/joeyorlando","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/9406895?v=4"},"committer":{"login":"web-flow","id":19864447,"profile_url":"https://github.com/web-flow","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/19864447?v=4"}},{"sha":"18695c1387be23097b27b6fbe5034ba3a2aa67cd","html_url":"https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/commit/18695c1387be23097b27b6fbe5034ba3a2aa67cd","commit":{"message":"feat(mcp-gateway): subscriptions/listen and x-mcp-header support (#6953) Continues the 2026-07-28 work after #6952. Now carries both remaining protocol features (#6954 was merged into this branch); Tasks stays separate (#6956). ## subscriptions/listen (SEP-2575) - New `routes/mcp-gateway/subscriptions.ts`: long-lived SSE stream handled at the route (the SDK transport only does single JSON responses). - Honors `toolsListChanged` only — tool lists are local DB, detected by fingerprint polling (20s); prompt/resource lists are upstream-aggregated, so those types are omitted from the ack per spec. - Ack-first ordering, subscription id (= listen request id) on every notification, graceful-close response, SSE keep-alives. - `tools.listChanged` now advertised `true` for 2026-07-28 clients (backed by the stream); legacy stays `false`. - Legacy clients calling the method get `-32601`; a listen without an id is rejected. ## x-mcp-header (SEP-2243) - New `clients/mcp-param-headers.ts`: annotation validation (token syntax, uniqueness, primitive types, static reachability) and value encoding (decimal ints, lowercase booleans, `=?base64?...?=` wrapper for unsafe values). - Invalid tool definitions are excluded from `tools/list` with a warning; valid annotations mirror argument values into `Mcp-Param-{name}` headers on upstream calls. - Per-call headers ride the passthrough-header pipeline; the existing credential-fingerprint check rebuilds pooled connections when the header set changes, so values can't leak across calls. - Assignment queries now project the tool input schema so the call path reads annotations without an extra lookup. ## Tests / checks - 9 unit + 4 real-socket route tests for subscriptions; 29 unit + 2 transport-level integration + 1 route test for x-mcp-header. - 396 pass across the gateway/client suites; `biome ci`, `tsc`, `knip`, docs link check clean. - Fixes the biome `noControlCharactersInRegex` error that failed #6954's CI (house ignore pattern on the RFC 9110 byte-range regex). ## Docs Gateway page: feature-table rows for change notifications and `x-mcp-header`, plus a client note for subscriptions.","author":{"name":"Joey Orlando","email":"joey@archestra.ai","date":"2026-07-29T14:51:31Z"},"committer":{"name":"GitHub","email":"noreply@github.com","date":"2026-07-29T14:51:31Z"}},"author":{"login":"joeyorlando","id":9406895,"profile_url":"https://github.com/joeyorlando","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/9406895?v=4"},"committer":{"login":"web-flow","id":19864447,"profile_url":"https://github.com/web-flow","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/19864447?v=4"}},{"sha":"40fe0314f3c722cb6358c48cd4dbecd3484cc798","html_url":"https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/commit/40fe0314f3c722cb6358c48cd4dbecd3484cc798","commit":{"message":"fix(llm-cost): price the OpenAI Codex models the registry omits (#6957) ## Summary models.dev carries the `gpt-5.3` generation onward but never backfilled the Codex and `chat-latest` models before it. Nothing resolves them, so each one reaches the fabricated default estimate: `gpt-5.1-codex` recorded at $50/M against a published $1.25/M, `gpt-5.1-codex-mini` at $30/M against $0.25/M — a 120× overstatement on a model people run all day. That estimate is not cosmetic. It flows into `interactions.cost`, the cost statistics, optimization-rule savings and token-cost limits. Prices for the eight affected ids are transcribed from OpenAI's own price list and placed at the bottom of the ladder, below the registry. The map can only fill what models.dev omits and cannot override an entry it already carries, so the 62 OpenAI rows the registry prices today cannot move. When the registry catches up the map stops being consulted and can be deleted; a PR adding these models upstream is the follow-up. Every id is stated outright rather than derived by stripping `-codex` to reach a base model. The suffix predicts the price for `gpt-5.1-codex`, which bills exactly what `gpt-5.1` does, and then breaks immediately on `gpt-5.1-codex-mini` at a fifth of it. Inferring a price from a name that resembles a sibling's is the failure this repo already removed once, for the family-matched AWS entries. The proxy's discovery path needed the same fill. It falls back to a first-party registry entry, which finds nothing for these models, so a discovered row kept the estimate for its whole life. That lookup ignores the provider the row was written under: the proxy records a discovered model against the *endpoint's* provider, so naming a Codex model on a Bedrock endpoint produces a `bedrock` row, and a reseller publishing no rate of its own has nothing better to offer than the model's own price. It also covers a second shape. models.dev publishes entries whose `cost` is an empty object, meaning the vendor sets no per-token rate — that entry resolves, so the row was previously enriched with its context and limits while the price alone fell through to the estimate. ## Verification Against the running app, a sync moves exactly the eight rows and nothing else — no row added, none removed, no other provider's price changed: ``` chat-latest 50.00/50.00 -> 5.00/30.00 gpt-5-chat-latest 50.00/50.00 -> 1.25/10.00 gpt-5-codex 50.00/50.00 -> 1.25/10.00 gpt-5.1-chat-latest 50.00/50.00 -> 1.25/10.00 gpt-5.1-codex 50.00/50.00 -> 1.25/10.00 gpt-5.1-codex-max 50.00/50.00 -> 1.25/10.00 gpt-5.1-codex-mini 30.00/30.00 -> 0.25/2.00 gpt-5.2-codex 50.00/50.00 -> 1.75/14.00 ``` The capability matrix carries the three new resolution paths. Its unpriced ratchet consults the published map, so a priced discovery row is not miscounted as falling through — the guard would otherwise quietly lose its meaning. ## Known gap These rows report `priceSource: "models_dev"`, which is wrong; the price came from OpenAI's list. Provenance is re-derived at read time by comparing the stored value against the AWS map rather than recorded when the price is written, so it cannot name a tier it does not know about. That predates this change — it already mislabels 48 Bedrock rows — and fixing it properly means recording the winning tier at write time. Left for that work rather than bolting a half-right label on here. --- ","author":{"name":"Alexander Balashov","email":"22360+divineforest@users.noreply.github.com","date":"2026-07-29T14:42:47Z"},"committer":{"name":"GitHub","email":"noreply@github.com","date":"2026-07-29T14:42:47Z"}},"author":{"login":"divineforest","id":22360,"profile_url":"https://github.com/divineforest","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/22360?v=4"},"committer":{"login":"web-flow","id":19864447,"profile_url":"https://github.com/web-flow","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/19864447?v=4"}},{"sha":"7bc0ff3262d277b328cd4d87370cc13193df6b8f","html_url":"https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/commit/7bc0ff3262d277b328cd4d87370cc13193df6b8f","commit":{"message":"fix(a2a): reject contentless message turns instead of sending them to the provider (#6959) ## Summary An A2A `SendMessage` whose only text part is empty or whitespace passed the execute gate but produced no current user turn, so the agent re-sent the conversation's prior context verbatim. Prior context always ends with the agent's last reply, so the request reached the provider terminating on an assistant message. Recent Claude models no longer support assistant prefill and reject such a request with a 400, which surfaced to users as the generic "There was an issue with your request. Please try again." The gate and the executor disagreed on what counts as content: `needToExecute` asks whether any part exists, while the executor builds a current user turn only from text that survives `trim()`. A blank text part satisfies the first and not the second. Blank text parts are now dropped when assembling `messageParts`, so both conditions read the same input. A contentless turn returns the existing `Nothing to execute` error (`-32602`), never reaches the provider, and no longer persists an empty user message into context history. A blank part mixed with real text also stops contributing a stray separator to the joined turn the model receives. Blank text falls through to the file branch rather than returning early, so a part carrying both blank text and a file keeps its payload — otherwise an attachment-only turn would be rejected, since `needToExecute` is evaluated before attachments are collected. Task resumption via `taskOps` is unaffected: it executes through `taskWasSwitchedToWorkingState`, independent of message parts. Known behavior change worth a reviewer's attention: a blank-text turn carrying an ephemeral execution prefix — chatops server-side sessions, where a 1:1 message has no text, no delivered attachment, and no skipped-attachment note — previously executed on the framing alone and now returns `Nothing to execute`. Found by auditing every prose-like `Archestra` occurrence across `frontend/src` and `backend/src` and classifying each as a genuine leak vs. a stable identifier. ## Backend Adds `archestraMcpBranding.appName`: a synchronous, gate-honoring accessor for call sites that cannot `await OrganizationModel.getAppName()`. Used in: - **Cost-limit block message** returned to any LLM proxy client. It deliberately leads with platform attribution ("blocked by X, not the AI provider"), which makes it exactly the line that must follow the brand. - **ChatOps** — welcome text, Teams install guidance, the agent-syntax tip, and the bot's own speaker label in thread history (Slack + Teams). `chatops-manager` already resolved the app name for mention matching but hardcoded it for display. Mention matching stays on the raw org value (permissive on purpose — people address the bot by whatever it's called); display now honors the enterprise gate. - **Agent email replies** — the `From` display name the recipient sees. - Read-only Vault resolution error, the OpenAPI auth description, and the web crawler's outbound `User-Agent`. ### Built-in MCP tool descriptions These are shipped strings frozen at module load, so they cannot read the branding singleton inline — it is only synced once an organization has been loaded. `getArchestraMcpTools()` already rebranded tool *names* at reconcile time; it now runs descriptions through the same swap. That covers every built-in at once rather than the handful that happen to name the brand today. The swap moves to `archestraMcpBranding.brandBuiltInText()` and `applyBuiltInSkillBranding()` delegates to it, so skills and tools cannot drift apart. It is case-sensitive, so lowercase `archestra.ai` URLs, `archestra__` inside longer identifiers, and env var names are untouched. ## Frontend - Threads `appName` through `ProxyBuildParams` so connect instructions read under the deployment's brand (the params object was already there, so this is a one-field change). - Brands the Bedrock IAM copy on the LLM provider form. - Passes `issuer` when enrolling TOTP, so an authenticator app labels the entry with the deployment's name instead of the default. Better Auth resolves the issuer as `body.issuer ?? options.issuer ?? context.appName`, and the latter two are fixed when the auth instance is constructed at import time — before any organization row can be read — so per-request is the only seam that works. **Existing enrollments keep their current label**; this only affects new ones. ## Deliberately unchanged Env vars, HTTP headers, token prefixes, `~/.archestra` paths and shell guard markers, archestra.ai/GitHub URLs, the `` wire tags, and log messages — all stable contracts or non-user-facing. The `archestra` **LLM provider**'s name and error strings also stay. That names the upstream product you're connecting to, alongside `openai`/`kimi`, not this deployment — branding it would be wrong when chaining to a genuine Archestra instance. Out of scope by request: the app-logo fallback and everything under `app-session-recording/`. ## Tests - `tool-description-branding.test.ts` (new) — built-in tool descriptions follow the brand under full white-labeling, and keep the default when the flag is off. - `clients.test.ts` — proxy connect instructions carry the app name, with no vendor brand left in the prose. - Existing `built-in-skill-branding` tests now transitively cover the shared helper. `pnpm lint`, `pnpm type-check`, and `pnpm knip` (dev + production) are clean; 781 tests across the touched backend suites and the frontend connection suite pass. ## Follow-up worth considering Most of these leaks were in files that *already* resolved the app name elsewhere. Verified against a live subscription: 13 of the 24 entries our static filter kept were rejected outright by `/chat/completions` with `model_not_supported` — retired aliases listed next to their still-working snapshots (`gpt-4` vs `gpt-4o`, `gpt-3.5-turbo` vs `gpt-3.5-turbo-0613`), client-internal agent models (`copilot-search-*`, `exec-agent-*`), and per-plan-unavailable models that still declare `"/chat/completions"` in `supported_endpoints`. No catalog field discriminates dead from alive entries (a dead alias can be field-identical to a working model, down to `version`), and on the verified plan every entry is `model_picker_enabled: false`, so no static filter can compute the usable set. GitHub's own clients avoid the problem only because their picker never exposes these entries. ## Fix **Verify invocability during model sync.** CAPI validates the model before the payload, so a deliberately invalid `{"model": …, "messages": []}` request is a zero-inference oracle: a dead model answers `model_not_supported`, a live one answers "messages must be non-empty". Nothing is generated and no model is ever invoked, so the probe cannot consume premium requests. The fetcher now probes every statically-kept candidate (8 concurrent) and drops only definite `model_not_supported` answers — 429/5xx/network failures keep the model, so an upstream outage degrades to the previous unverified catalog rather than an empty one. Runs everywhere the fetcher is used: connect-time key validation, lazy re-sync, explicit sync, and the proxy `/models` listing. **Actionable error for the residual window.** A conversation can stay pinned to a model that has since died (the proxy's error wrapping keeps `message`/`type` but drops the upstream `code`). The chat error mapper now classifies Copilot's model-not-supported 400 as `NotFound` — "The selected model is not available. Please choose a different model." — instead of the retry-suggesting invalid-request copy, which misleads on a deterministic rejection. ## Testing - New proxy route tests drive the real adapter and Copilot fetch wrapper (token exchange + editor-identity headers) against a faked wire, pinning that the catalogued model name goes upstream and the upstream 400 surfaces for both streaming and non-streaming. - New chat stream test pins that a github-copilot conversation's model FK is dereferenced to the provider model name before dispatch. - Fetcher tests cover the verification: a listed-but-rejected model is dropped, probes only target statically-kept candidates, inconclusive probes (429/network) keep the model. - Error-mapper tests cover the NotFound classification and that other Copilot 400s keep the generic invalid-request code. - Live validation on a dev stack with a real subscription: synced catalog went from 24 models (13 dead) to the invocable set; The timer was the MCP SDK's default request timeout in the app iframe's guest client: the SDK passed no request options to `callServerTool`, and nothing downstream was stricter, so the guest always lost the race while the backend kept generating (and the proxy kept billing) a result nobody would receive. Live measurement on a dev stack: the app showed the error at exactly 60s while the same completion returned HTTP 200 at 100s and was recorded in LLM logs ~40s after the app had already failed. The guest now bounds host tool calls at 10 minutes, matching the platform's own upstream LLM client ceiling (`ANTHROPIC_CLIENT_TIMEOUT_MS`) rather than gating stricter than it. Cancellation travels the whole chain: the guest's timeout or teardown aborts the host bridge's fetch via the `oncalltool` handler's `extra.signal`; the app proxy route closes the per-request transport when the client disconnects, which makes the protocol abort the in-flight handler's signal; that signal reaches `executeArchestraTool` (as the existing `context.abortSignal`) and `executeToolCallForOwner` (its existing `abortSignal` option); and an aborted LLM completion stops quietly instead of logging an error and claiming `llm_unavailable`. Two route-level details deserve reviewer attention. In JSON-response mode an aborted handler never produces a response, so `transport.handleRequest` never settles — the route races it against the client-disconnect path instead of awaiting it bare. And an aborted request leaves its transport closed mid-flight, so the per-(app,user) cached server is evicted rather than released for reuse; the cache's exclusive `acquire` guarantees the closed transport can only ever belong to the aborted request. ## Validation - `app-sdk-runtime.test.ts`: the guest-module stub now honors the MCP SDK's request-options timeout contract; new tests pin that a 3-minute completion resolves (red before this fix, failing with the exact reported error) and that a completion beyond the 10-minute ceiling still times out. - `app-llm.test.ts`: an aborted call cancels the model call and reports cancellation, not a provider failure. - Live on a dev stack with a reasoning model (glm-5.1): a 188-second completion resolves in the real iframe chain where it previously died at 60s; killing the viewer 25 seconds into a call produced the cancelled tool-call record within ~1 second. ## Follow-up The LLM proxy's non-streaming handlers do not tie their own upstream request to their client's disconnect, so a cancelled completion can still run to completion inside the proxy and record the interaction (observed landing two minutes after the abort). That gap predates this change, spans every provider adapter, and equally affects non-streamed chat cancellation — left for its own change. No docs change: the apps page never promised a timeout, and the fix restores its documented behavior (`llm.complete` resolves to the model's text). --- ","state":"closed","draft":false,"merged":false,"html_url":"https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/pull/6963","user":{"login":"piercypixel","id":13911621,"profile_url":"https://github.com/piercypixel","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/13911621?v=4"},"requested_reviewers":["iskhakov"],"head":{"ref":"piercypixel/t981-app-reasoning-timeout","sha":"16d15550f6fcc7dfed3fd8a0147db610cc340941","repo":{"full_name":"archestra-ai/archestra","description":"Enterprise AI Platform with guardrails, MCP registry, gateway & orchestrator"}},"base":{"ref":"main","sha":"1a1fd231e171822cd869f84c7e3346b59e76fbfb","repo":{"full_name":"archestra-ai/archestra","description":"Enterprise AI Platform with guardrails, MCP registry, gateway & orchestrator"}},"created_at":"2026-07-29T16:38:35Z","updated_at":"2026-07-29T17:06:40Z","closed_at":"2026-07-29T17:06:38Z","merged_at":"2026-07-29T17:06:38Z"},{"number":6962,"title":"fix(llm-pricing): read Amazon's global-endpoint price marker for Nova","body":"## Summary The vendored AWS snapshot identifies a global-endpoint SKU by a `_Global` suffix on the usage type. That is Anthropic's and TwelveLabs' convention. Amazon's own Nova models mark it `-cross-region-global` instead, so no global entry was ever transcribed for them — and worse, the single entry that was transcribed crossed the two tiers: `Nova 2.0 Lite` held a regional input beside a global output, a pair AWS charges at neither endpoint. `Nova 2.0 Omni` was wrong the same way. `Nova 2.0 Pro` had a correct regional entry but no global one, so a `global.` profile silently paid the regional rate. Re-read from the offer document, standard on-demand, text dimensions only: | model | regional | global | |---|---|---| | Nova 2.0 Lite | 0.33 / 2.75 | 0.30 / 2.50 | | Nova 2.0 Omni | 0.30 / 2.80 | 0.30 / 2.50 | | Nova 2.0 Pro | 1.375 / 11 | 1.25 / 10 | Omni's input is genuinely the same on both tiers; only its output carries the premium. It does not follow the uniform 1.1× uplift the Claude listings show, which is why the values are read per dimension rather than derived from one. A sweep of both offer documents confirms the split is exactly these three models: everything else publishing a global SKU uses `_Global`. `Nova Sonic 2.0` is deliberately untouched. It splits its dimensions by modality, and the stored 0.33/2.75 is its text pair; the 3.00 sitting beside it is `speech-input-tokens` and belongs to a different meter. Both conventions are now recorded in the transcription rules, since reading either one wrongly produces a price that looks plausible. ## Verification A test asserts the regional and global tiers resolve to different prices for `amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0`; it fails against the previous snapshot, where both ids collapsed onto the one mixed entry. A standing guard asserts no `|global` entry is priced above its regional counterpart — crossing the tiers is what produced an entry neither endpoint bills at. It covers all ten global entries. `Nova 2.0 Omni` and `Nova 2.0 Pro` have no `AWS_PRICE_IDENTITY` mapping yet, so their entries are latent until a deployment serves those ids; `Nova 2.0 Lite` is mapped and live. --- ","state":"open","draft":false,"merged":false,"html_url":"https://github.com/archestra-ai/archestra/pull/6962","user":{"login":"divineforest","id":22360,"profile_url":"https://github.com/divineforest","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/22360?v=4"},"head":{"ref":"fix/bedrock-nova-global-endpoint-prices","sha":"9b39445016b511141ba55bf847076ba37492124a","repo":{"full_name":"archestra-ai/archestra","description":"Enterprise AI Platform with guardrails, MCP registry, gateway & orchestrator"}},"base":{"ref":"main","sha":"2cb4a589217f3511054924e1e5e8e5de7b290b72","repo":{"full_name":"archestra-ai/archestra","description":"Enterprise AI Platform with guardrails, MCP registry, gateway & orchestrator"}},"created_at":"2026-07-29T15:09:53Z","updated_at":"2026-07-29T15:10:05Z"},{"number":6961,"title":"fix(llm-cost): stop rounding model prices to the cent before costing them","body":"## Summary `getEffectivePricing` formatted the per-million price with `toFixed(2)`, and every cost path parses that string back: `interactions.cost` via `kb-interaction.ts`, token-cost limits in `limit.ts`, and optimization-rule savings in `cost-optimization.ts`. The rounding is therefore a billing error rather than a display choice. A model published at $0.035/M was costed at $0.04 — 14% high across 45 rows today — and anything under $0.005/M would have recorded as free. Storage was never the problem. The columns are `numeric(20,12)` and hold `0.000000035` exactly; the precision died at the read boundary. Cache prices already had this fix, with a comment stating that 2-decimal rounding "would be materially lossy here". Input and output simply never got the same treatment, which is why the models table has been rendering `$1.00` beside an unpadded `$0.1` cache price all along. The helper is now shared rather than cache-specific. Padding moves to the reading end, so `$50.00` still renders as `$50.00` while `$0.035` survives intact, and all four price columns agree. Every display site goes through one formatter: the models table, the model select, and the chat model tooltip. The default and no-token-rate tiers keep their `"50.00"` / `"0.00"` literals — two decimals is their full precision, so passing them through the formatter would churn the suite for no gain. ## Verification A sub-cent row was added to the capability matrix (`bedrock/amazon.nova-micro`, published at $0.035/M by both AWS and the registry). Under the old formatting it reads $0.04 and the row fails, so it pins the regression it names rather than the formatting alone. It's only reachable inside the "Add API Key" dialog (ChatGPT as an auth-method radio revealed after picking OpenAI; Copilot/M365 as entries in an API-key provider dropdown), and no copy anywhere says "use the ChatGPT Plus/Pro subscription you already pay for". The chat empty state is API-key-framed too. Proposal: make "sign in with a subscription you already pay for" a first-class, discoverable path. Add a "Use your subscription" entry point next to "Add API Key" (and mirror it in the chat first-run empty state), limited to the three existing subscription providers, and list connected subscriptions in a personal "Your connections" section instead of the anonymous org keys table. This is a UX/IA change only — device flows, per-user credential storage, and scoping stay as-is. Full design below. Full design proposal ## Goals - Make "sign in with a subscription you already pay for" a first-class, discoverable setup path. - One flow that serves both personas: the first admin setting up a fresh org and every later member linking their own account (all three device flows are already self-service, `access-control.ts:939-955`). - Separate the mental models: org-shared API keys vs personal subscription connections. ## Non-goals (v1) - No new providers. Scope is the existing three: ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365 Copilot. (Claude Pro/Max explicitly out — Anthropic's ToS prohibits third-party reuse; opencode removed it.) - No admin oversight of members' connections (see Follow-ups). - No changes to chat beyond the first-run empty state — no model-selector changes; the reactive auth-required card stays as error recovery. - No backend/protocol changes: device flows, per-user credential storage, and security scoping stay as-is. This is a UX/IA change. ## Design ### 1. Model-providers screen: two entry points `/llm/model-providers` gets a second primary button next to "Add API Key": > **Use your subscription** - "Add API Key" keeps the existing dialog, but it becomes purely about API keys: the OpenAI form loses the ChatGPT-subscription radio; `github-copilot` and `microsoft-365-copilot` leave its provider dropdown. Single path per credential type — subscriptions are not reachable through the API-key dialog anymore. - "Use your subscription" opens a new dialog in the same visual style as the existing API-key dialog: a provider select limited to the three subscription providers, then that provider's sign-in (existing device-flow components) inline. Success creates the personal-scope key exactly as today. ### 2. "Your connections" section Connected subscriptions no longer render as anonymous rows in the org keys table. The model-providers page gets a personal **Your connections** section (above or beside the keys table) showing each connected subscription with provider logo, plan wording, and a disconnect action. This makes per-user vs org-shared visually obvious. The org keys table remains for API keys. ### 3. Chat first-run empty state The zero-keys empty state mirrors the split: two buttons — "Use your subscription" and "Add API key" — opening the same two dialogs. The rest of first-run onboarding (default-model step) is unchanged. ### 4. Copy principles - Always name the plans, not the protocol: "ChatGPT (Plus/Pro/Team)", "GitHub Copilot", "Microsoft 365 Copilot". - Lead with the value: "Sign in with an account you already pay for — no API key needed." - Keep the per-user framing explicit: "Connections are personal — each teammate signs in with their own account." ## Compatibility Existing personal keys created through the old paths keep working untouched — this is a UI/IA reorganization; storage, scoping, and proxy behavior are unchanged. Docs (`platform-supported-llm-providers.md`) need a pass to lead with the subscription path. ## Follow-ups (explicitly out of v1) 1. **Admin visibility/governance**: let admins see (and possibly revoke) which members have connected which subscription. 2. **In-chat discovery**: model selector could advertise not-yet-connected subscription providers ("ChatGPT — sign in to use your subscription") and replace the "No models available" dead end with a connect CTA. 3. **More providers**: Gemini/Google, GitLab Duo, etc., as they become feasible. Reference: opencode's `/connect` flow, where "ChatGPT Plus/Pro" is a first-class auth choice. All are reproducible from linked harnesses; independent verification welcome. This issue runs long (I know brevity is the ask), but it's proposing a wire-format change and the token / comprehension / losslessness trade-offs are the whole case. I've front-loaded them and kept the rest skimmable. The comparisons are sourced, reproducible trade-offs measured on your specific data shapes; I've let the numbers stand on their own. ## Proposal Archestra already compresses tool-result messages before forwarding them to the model (`convertToolResultsToToon`, gated on "only if it actually saves tokens"). I'd like to add **GCF** (Graph Compact Format) as a *selectable* encoder alongside TOON, **off by default**, so nothing changes unless an operator opts in. Archestra only encodes (never decodes) tool results, so the entire effect is token reduction with no downstream parsing risk. I've already built it as a small, additive change (details in "Proposed design" below and on the branch above). Opening this as an issue first because it touches a format you chose and shipped, and I'd rather get your read on the approach (and let you shape the design) before asking for review time. Precedent is in "Adoption" below, including OmniRoute, a platform/gateway that's the closest analog to this proposal. ## Benchmark (archestra tool-result shapes) Three-way (JSON / TOON / GCF), compact-JSON baseline, representative MCP tool-result payloads, measured with **archestra's own tokenizers**: `cl100k_base` (its `TiktokenTokenizer`: OpenAI/Cohere/Gemini/Bedrock/ZhipuAI/Minimax) and `@anthropic-ai/tokenizer` (its `AnthropicTokenizer`), plus `o200k_base` for newer GPT-4o/5. Every GCF output verified lossless via `decodeGeneric` (15/15). `@blackwell-systems/gcf` 2.2.2, `@toon-format/toon` ^2.1.0. **Cross-tokenizer average (uniform shapes):** | Tokenizer | GCF vs JSON | GCF vs TOON | TOON vs JSON | |---|--:|--:|--:| | `cl100k_base` (most providers) | **31.2%** | 7.9% | 23.4% | | `@anthropic-ai/tokenizer` | **32.4%** | 3.2% | 29.3% | | `o200k_base` (GPT-4o/5) | **31.5%** | 8.0% | 23.7% | GCF cuts JSON tokens **~31–32% across every tokenizer archestra uses** (robust, not a single-tokenizer artifact). (Consistent with the broader GCF 43-tokenizer merge-rate study across 20 providers; the two tokenizer families archestra actually runs already confirm it.) **Per shape (cl100k_base):** | Shape | JSON | TOON | GCF | GCF vs JSON | GCF vs TOON | |---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | db_users [100] | 4603 | 3117 | 3123 | 32.2% | −0.2% | | k8s_pods [100] | 4952 | 2821 | 2878 | 41.9% | −2.0% | | github_issues [50] | 3053 | 2368 | 2274 | 25.5% | 4.0% | | cloud_cost [100] | 3981 | 2595 | 2502 | 37.2% | 3.6% | | prometheus_series [500] | 6494 | 5498 | 4505 | 30.6% | 18.1% | | orders_nested [50] | 3451 | **3750** | 2578 | 25.3% | **31.3%** | Where GCF pulls ahead of TOON (and how it holds across tokenizers): - **Nested tool results: GCF beats TOON +18–31% under *every* tokenizer.** TOON goes *negative* vs JSON here (−8.7%), so archestra's "only compress if it saves tokens" gate would skip TOON and capture nothing; GCF still saves ~25%. Archestra gateways arbitrary MCP tool outputs (many nested/mixed), so this is real captured savings. - **Flat uniform rows are a wash** with TOON (within ~2%, a fixed header cost that doesn't scale), no regression. - **Numeric/time-series**: GCF ~+18% vs TOON under OpenAI tokenizers; roughly parity under Anthropic's, a tokenizer-specific effect, not claimed as a general win. ## Comprehension (the savings don't cost accuracy) Fewer tokens only helps if the model still reads the payload correctly, the whole point for a gateway that feeds tool results to LLMs. GCF is validated on that directly (published eval suite: 2,400+ LLM evaluations across 11 models and 3 providers, [gcformat.com/guide/benchmarks](https://gcformat.com/guide/benchmarks.html)): - **Generic profile (what this proposal uses): 100% comprehension on every frontier model.** No format instructions or fine-tuning required. - On structurally hard payloads the gap over TOON widens: **GCF 91.2% vs TOON 68.8% vs JSON 54.1%.** - Generation validity 5/5 on every frontier model (vs TOON ~1/5); archestra only encodes, so comprehension is the load-bearing result here. ## Losslessness and safety (why the encoding choice matters for a gateway) - **GCF is provably lossless; TOON is not.** A 10M-round-trip fuzz of `@toon-format/toon` ([harness](https://github.com/blackwell-systems/gcf/blob/main/eval/toon-fuzz.mjs), [raw log](https://github.com/blackwell-systems/gcf/blob/main/eval/results/toon-fuzz-10M-2026-06-16.log)) recorded **176,487 silent corruptions and 577,717 decode errors, 7.54% failure** (92.46% success). Root cause: TOON's encoder doesn't quote strings containing `[ ] { } :`, so the decoder misparses them (e.g. `"name[3]: a,b,c"` decodes to `["a","b","c"]`). Clean uniform rows round-trip fine, but tool results routinely carry such strings: log lines, stack traces, error messages, code, embedded JSON. GCF quotes ambiguous strings by grammar: 43B+ round-trips, **0 failures**. Reproduce: `node eval/toon-fuzz.mjs 10000000`. - **Structural-injection resistance** (relevant to archestra's guardrails / trusted-data model). A controlled study of the "delimiter dissolution" attack ([eval/stoon-injection-study](https://github.com/blackwell-systems/gcf/blob/main/eval/results/stoon-injection-study.md)) shows attacker-controlled string content in a record can be re-parsed as trusted structure under TOON (up to 90% leak on some open models, 0% under a JSON control). **GCF is the only format tested whose leak rate never exceeds the JSON baseline on any model.** A gateway compresses tool results that often originate from untrusted MCP servers/external APIs, so the encoding must not dissolve the boundary between data and structure. Net: **~31% fewer tokens than JSON with no comprehension penalty, provable losslessness, and no new injection surface**, versus TOON, which saves fewer tokens on nested data, scores lower on comprehension, silently corrupts a measurable fraction of values, and widens the structural-injection surface. ## Proposed design (already implemented on the branch) - New backend config field `config.llmProxy.toolResultCompressionFormat` (env `ARCHESTRA_LLM_PROXY_TOOL_RESULT_COMPRESSION_FORMAT`, `toon` | `gcf`), **default `toon`**, additive and opt-in, so no existing deployment changes behavior. - **TOON is left untouched.** Each of the 7 provider adapters keeps its `toonEncode` import and calls; GCF is a parallel branch at the existing call site: `const compressed = preferGcf() ? encodeGcf(parsed) : toonEncode(parsed);`. A small GCF-only util (`preferGcf()`, `encodeGcf()`) holds the format check and encoder. - The existing per-org/team `convertToolResultsToToon` toggle (whether to compress) and the token-savings gate (skip if not smaller) are unchanged; this only adds *which* encoder can run. - `@blackwell-systems/gcf` pinned exactly to `2.2.2` (published 2026-06-30, clears the 7-day `minimumReleaseAge`). Zero runtime dependencies. - A follow-up could promote the format from a config flag to a per-org/team setting + UI (mirroring the existing `convertToolResultsToToon` column), kept separate to stay reviewable. ## Adoption GCF is in production across a range of projects, including several platform/gateway integrations like archestra's: - **[Chrome DevTools MCP](https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp)** (46K★, Google Chrome DevTools team): `--experimentalDataFormat=gcf`. - **[OmniRoute](https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute)** (6.1K★), AI gateway; vendored GCF's encoder into its compression engine. Closest analog to this proposal. - **[Speakeasy](https://github.com/speakeasy-api/openapi)**: `oq --format gcf`, merged after a dependency/security audit. - **[NetClaw](https://github.com/automateyournetwork/netclaw)** (556★): switched from TOON to GCF after benchmarking on its own network data. - **[ctx](https://github.com/stevesolun/ctx)** (510★), **NeuroNest** (commercial agent IDE), **Open Data Products SDK** (Linux Foundation), **[Raycast](https://raycast.com/blackwell-systems/json-to-gcf-converter)** Store extension, and others. Full list: https://gcformat.com/ecosystem/adopters.html ## Research & further reading - **Website / playground / docs:** https://gcformat.com, including [playground](https://gcformat.com/playground.html) (paste your own data for a live JSON/TOON/GCF diff), [benchmarks](https://gcformat.com/guide/benchmarks.html), [GCF vs TOON](https://gcformat.com/guide/vs-toon.html), [tokenizer analysis](https://gcformat.com/guide/tokenizer-analysis.html), [independent AI reviews](https://gcformat.com/reviews/). - **Spec & whitepaper:** [SPEC v3.2](https://github.com/blackwell-systems/gcf/blob/main/SPEC.md) (173 conformance fixtures, zero runtime deps, MIT) · [whitepaper](https://github.com/blackwell-systems/gcf/blob/main/gcf-whitepaper.pdf). - **Papers (Zenodo DOIs):** - GCF: A Token-Optimized Wire Format for Structured LLM Interactions, [10.5281/zenodo.20579817](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20579817) - Tokenizer-Attention Coupling: How BPE Merge Decisions Permanently Shape Transformer Internal Organization, [10.5281/zenodo.20925910](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20925910) - Stranded Attention: BPE Tokenization Permanently Constrains Transformer Structural Capacity, [10.5281/zenodo.21158886](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21158886) - Developmental Atlas of Attention Head Specialization: Spacing, Stranding, and the Capacity Tax of BPE Tokenization, [10.5281/zenodo.21205389](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21205389) ## The ask Would you accept GCF as an opt-in tool-result format on these terms (default TOON, additive, zero-dep)? If yes, I'll open the PR from the ready branch. If you'd rather a different shape, tell me and I'll build to your preference before you spend review time: a per-team setting instead of a config flag, no new dependency (GCF's TS source is zero-dep and vendorable), or whatever fits. Repro: 1. Configure a tool like `read_issue`. 2. Set Tool Call Policy so the call is allowed. 3. Set Tool Result Policy to `Blocked`. 4. Enable `Treat context as sensitive from the start of chat`. 5. Ask the agent to read an issue. Expected: The tool call may execute, but the result content should be replaced before it is sent to the model. Entry point Add a mode switch to the header of the `Tool Call Policies` and `Tool Result Policies` sections: - `Current` - `Historical impact` In `Current`, everything works as it does today. Draft mode inside the existing UI In `Historical impact` mode: - the policy cards remain visually similar; - changes are written only to a local candidate set; - a clear banner indicates that live policies are unchanged and that this is no-LLM / no live tool execution; - a button appears: - `Run on recent history` This keeps the new functionality in the place where it is meant to be used and preserves the current UI structure. ## Result output The result should show a compact summary: - `Affected sessions` - `Affected tool calls` - `Newly blocked` - `Newly require approval` - `Trust-state changed` - `Unknown / missing context` For `Tool Result Policies`, additionally: - `Results reclassified` - `First downstream affected step` - `Blocked after trust change` - `Approval required after trust change` ### Explanation layer It is important to show not only how many cases are affected, but also why. parts.text: Build me an app that helps new developers understand any GitHub repository in minutes. Enter a repository and let AI explain the project structure, key contributors, important files, development timeline, and where to start contributing, using real GitHub data.

Optimize the repository scan for speed and accuracy. Fetch GitHub data in parallel, minimize unnecessary API calls, and cache data during the current session for faster loading. Always use real GitHub MCP data to analyze the codebase, files, contributors, branches, commits, and pull requests. Never generate fake or placeholder information. If some data isn't available, clearly display "Data unavailable" instead of making assumptions.

Improve the UI with a modern, polished design and add more real repository insights. Fix all sections that are not loading correctly, ensure every field fetches accurate GitHub MCP data, never use placeholder data, and show **"Data unavailable"** when a specific field cannot be retrieved.

Fix the **Overview**, **Key Guide**, and **Where to Contribute** sections. They are incorrectly showing **"Data unavailable"** for repositories that contain sufficient information. Improve the GitHub MCP data fetching and AI analysis so these sections generate accurate summaries from the repository's README, project structure, files, commits, contributors, issues, and pull requests. Only show **"Data unavailable"** when the required GitHub data truly cannot be retrieved.

Improve the app with a more modern, polished UI and make all sections fully functional. Fix the **Project Structure**, **Architecture**, **Workflow**, **Overview**, **Key Guide**, and **Where to Contribute** sections so they analyze and display real GitHub MCP data instead of showing unavailable data whenever possible. Add richer insights such as the folder structure, key files, tech stack, dependencies, contributor roles, development timeline, code statistics, and onboarding recommendations. Never use placeholder data, and only show **"Data unavailable"** when the GitHub MCP tools genuinely cannot retrieve the information.

Improve the app with a premium, modern UI using glassmorphism, smooth animations, better typography, icons, responsive layouts, interactive cards, and a clean developer-focused design. Fix the **Project Structure**, **Architecture**, **Workflow**, **Overview**, **Key Guide**, and **Where to Contribute** sections so they display real GitHub MCP data whenever available. Add richer insights such as folder structure, key files, tech stack, dependencies, contributor roles, development timeline, and code statistics. Never use placeholder data, and only show **"Data unavailable"** when the GitHub MCP tools genuinely cannot retrieve the information.

Fix the **Good First Issues & Beginner Tasks** section. Instead of always showing **"Data unavailable"**, fetch real GitHub issues labeled `good first issue`, `help wanted`, `beginner`, or similar labels using the GitHub MCP tools. Display those issues when available, and only show **"Data unavailable"** if the repository genuinely has no beginner-friendly issues or the data cannot be retrieved.

Fix the **Project Structure**, **Files**, **Architecture**, and **Issues** sections. They are incorrectly showing **"Data unavailable"** for repositories that contain this information. Ensure the app fetches the real file tree, folders, key files, repository structure, and open issues through the GitHub MCP tools. If a repository doesn't expose a specific field, handle it gracefully and only show **"Data unavailable"** when the data truly cannot be retrieved. Never use placeholder or fabricated data.

Enhance the AI analysis to provide deeper, repository-specific insights. Explain the project architecture, identify the purpose of key folders and files, summarize the development workflow, detect the main technologies and dependencies, highlight important entry points, and recommend where new contributors should start. Base every insight on real GitHub MCP data and repository contents. Make the analysis accurate, detailed, and unique for each repository instead of using generic summaries.

enhancement.prompt: Build me an app that uses AI and real GitHub data to help new developers understand any repository by breaking down its project structure, key files, dependencies, development timeline, and beginner-friendly issues to show them exactly where to start contributing.
enhancement.response:
RepoLens AI is built and ready to help you explore and understand any GitHub codebase in minutes.

- Fetches and analyzes real-time repository data using GitHub integration, including file trees, README files, commits, contributors, and pull requests without placeholder fallbacks.
- Breaks down project structure, key architecture, and important entry points so you instantly grasp how the codebase is organized.
- Surfaces real beginner-friendly issues like `good first issue` and `help wanted` tags to guide your onboarding.
- Highlights active contributors, development workflows, and tech stack details for a complete project overview.
- Employs parallel data-fetching and caching for fast, responsive loading across all tabs and sections.

Type any public repository name (like `facebook/react` or `torvalds/linux`) into the search bar to run your first repository analysis.
